title: Open port 8790 on 192.168.1.156's firewall for the engine
description:
What the engine checked from its own host: 192.168.1.156 is reachable from the engine host (it answers on port 22, 8006) but port 8790 times out — the port is being dropped by a firewall on that host.

On Proxmox that is the host firewall. This opens port 8790 to 192.168.1.0/24 only (the helper still requires the token), then shows the firewall state:
```bash
pve-firewall status; ss -tlnp | grep 8790
pvesh create /nodes/$(hostname)/firewall/rules --type in --action ACCEPT --proto tcp --dport 8790 --source 192.168.1.0/24 --enable 1 --comment 'scaffold local runner'
sleep 3; pve-firewall status
```
If `pve-firewall status` says **disabled**, the drop is elsewhere — paste the output of `iptables -S INPUT | head -20; nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -n 8790` instead.
Done when the paste shows the ACCEPT rule for port 8790 and pve-firewall status says enabled/running — I re-check the connection from the engine on every paste.

_Engine capability repair: local_runner port_filtered_

title: Set up Pi-hole as the home network's DNS, blocking ads and trackers
description:
The operator asked for this directly: "there should of been a portion regarding creating security for the home lab including pi hole". It was never in the plan — the brief asked for "the best possible security" and that was never turned into anything concrete, so this is new work, not a repair.

Goal: every device in the house resolves names through Pi-hole, so ads, trackers and known malicious domains are blocked for the whole network — phones and TVs included, with nothing to install on them.

Put it in its own unprivileged LXC on the Proxmox host with a STATIC address, because every device on the network will depend on it. Read the host for what is already there rather than asking: `pct list` shows the containers in use and the addresses in use.

Two things the operator must not be left to discover:
  - If Pi-hole is the only resolver and its container is down, the whole house loses DNS. Say in plain words what happens then and how they get back (a second resolver, or the router's own DNS as a fallback), and set it up.
  - Blocklists that are too aggressive break things people actually use. Start with the default lists, and say how to unblock one thing when something breaks.

They are not expected to know the technology. Do not ask them which blocklists to use or which DNS upstream to pick — choose sensible ones, name them, and say what each means for them.

Done when a device on the LAN resolves through Pi-hole and a known ad domain comes back blocked.

FACTS READ OFF THE HOST just now — use these, do not ask for them:

  IDs ALREADY TAKEN (Proxmox shares one id space between containers and VMs — `pct list` and `qm list` together):
    containers 101 jellyfin, 102 prowlarr, 103 radarr, 104 sonarr, 105 download-client, 111 control-panel, 120 caddy-proxy
    VMs        100 gpu-vm, 106 palworld-server, 110 ai-vm
    So 100 is NOT free — use 130, which is free.

  STORAGE (`pvesm status`):
    local      dir      — this is the one that holds container templates (vztmpl)
    local-lvm  lvmthin  — container/VM disks; use this for an 8G rootfs
    oasis      zfspool  — the 5.7 TB media pool, NOT for this container's rootfs

  NETWORK (`ip route`, `ip -4 addr`):
    subnet 192.168.1.0/24, gateway 192.168.1.1, bridge vmbr0, the host itself is 192.168.1.156
    static addresses already in use on the LAN: .21 prowlarr, .22 radarr, .23 sonarr, .25 control-panel, .156 the host
    192.168.1.30 does not answer a ping, so use that for Pi-hole.

  So: CTID 130, template storage `local`, rootfs on `local-lvm`, ip=192.168.1.30/24, gw=192.168.1.1.

TWO THINGS THE PREVIOUS DRAFT GOT WRONG — do not repeat them:
  1. Its `--net0` was `name=eth0,ip=...,gw=...` with NO `bridge=`. A container NIC with no bridge is not attached to anything: Pi-hole would install into something with no network and the whole step would look like it worked. It must be `--net0 name=eth0,bridge=vmbr0,ip=192.168.1.30/24,gw=192.168.1.1`.
  2. It offered CTID 100, which is the gpu-vm. Check the id against BOTH lists before using it.

One caveat to tell the operator in plain words, because it is the thing that bites later: 192.168.1.30 is free right now, but if the Spectrum router's DHCP range includes it, the router could hand the same address to a phone one day and the house would lose DNS intermittently. Say that, and tell them where to look on the router to confirm the DHCP range starts above .30 — or to reserve .30 for Pi-hole there.

DO NOT ENABLE PI-HOLE'S DHCP SERVER IN THIS STEP. The previous draft ended with
    pct exec 130 -- pihole -a enabledhcp 192.168.1.50 192.168.1.200 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0 86400
which turns Pi-hole into a DHCP server handing out 192.168.1.50–200 on a LAN that already has one — the Spectrum router. Two DHCP servers on one network produce intermittent failures that are miserable to diagnose: some devices get an address from one, some from the other, and it looks like random WiFi trouble for weeks.

This step's job is DNS only: a Pi-hole that resolves and filters, reachable at its static address. How devices come to USE it is ADD112's job, and there the ROUTER hands out Pi-hole's address as the DNS server. Pi-hole-as-DHCP is the FALLBACK in ADD112, used only if the Spectrum firmware refuses a custom DNS server — and if it is ever used, the router's own DHCP must be turned OFF first, in the same breath, never both at once.

So: no `enabledhcp`, no `--dhcp`, nothing that hands out addresses. Finish with Pi-hole answering queries on 192.168.1.30 and nothing else changed about the network.

WHAT THE LAST ATTEMPT GOT WRONG — read off the machine, do not repeat it:

  1. It ran `pveam update && pveam list local | grep debian-12` and that command NEEDS ROOT. This runner executes WRITES with sudo but READS unprivileged, so the output was a permission refusal (`ipcc_send_rec[1] failed`, `Unable to load access control list`, rc=1) — not a statement about the system. Do not put a privileged `pveam`/`pvesm`/`pct config` READ in this step: it will fail and it is not needed.
  2. Having failed that read, it went straight to `pct create` WITHOUT downloading the template. The create genuinely ran, made the logical volume and the filesystem, then rolled back:
        volume 'local:vztmpl/debian-12-standard_12.7-1_amd64.tar.zst' does not exist
        unable to create CT 130
    The template has to be FETCHED before the container can be built from it.

SO: `pveam download local debian-12-standard_12.7-1_amd64.tar.zst` is a WRITE and runs with sudo, which means it is allowed and it is all that is needed — no listing, no availability check. Put it immediately before `pct create`, and let the create be the thing that proves the template arrived. If the exact filename has moved on, the download failing says so plainly and that is a better signal than a refused read.

Everything else about the last attempt was right and should be kept: CTID 130, `local:vztmpl/…` for the template, `--rootfs local-lvm:8`, `--net0 name=eth0,bridge=vmbr0,ip=192.168.1.30/24,gw=192.168.1.1`, `--unprivileged 1`, `--onboot 1`, the Pi-hole unattended install, `pihole -a -p $MASS_PASSWORD`, and NO DHCP.

THE TEMPLATE NAME, READ OFF THE HOST — the operator has now granted the runner root for `pveam` reads, so this is measured, not remembered:

  $ pveam available --section system
    system          debian-12-standard_12.12-1_amd64.tar.zst

The name is `debian-12-standard_12.12-1_amd64.tar.zst`. The previous attempt used `debian-12-standard_12.7-1_amd64.tar.zst`, which Proxmox answered with "no such template" — that version was invented. Use the measured name in BOTH the download and the `local:vztmpl/…` path of `pct create`, and do not write a version number you have not read.

`pveam available` now works through the runner, so if the name has moved again, read it rather than guess.

WHERE THIS STEP ACTUALLY IS NOW — read off the host, so do not redo what is done:

  $ pct list            -> 130 exists
  $ pct exec 130 -- ip -4 addr show eth0
      inet 192.168.1.30/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global eth0
  $ pct exec 130 -- ls /etc/pihole
      ls: cannot access '/etc/pihole': No such file or directory

So container 130 is BUILT, running, and on the right address. The template is downloaded and cached. What is left is Pi-hole itself, which is not installed.

Guard the create rather than repeating it — `pct status 130 >/dev/null 2>&1 || pct create 130 …` — so re-running this step finishes it instead of colliding with its own earlier work. Same for `pct start`: `pct status 130 | grep -q running || pct start 130`.

WHY THE INSTALL FAILED, and what actually fixes it: `curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | bash /dev/stdin --unattended` dropped into Pi-hole's interactive dialog anyway and exited —
      Please continue when the static addressing has been configured.
      [i] Installer exited
`--unattended` does not mean "answer the questions for me": it means "read the answers from /etc/pihole/setupVars.conf and do not ask". With no such file there is nothing to read, so it shows the dialog. WRITE THAT FILE FIRST, then run the installer unattended.

It needs at least the interface, the static address and gateway this container already has (eth0, 192.168.1.30/24, 192.168.1.1), the upstream resolvers to forward to, whether to install the web interface and the web server, whether to log queries, and the privacy level. Use the values already measured above rather than asking. Write it with `printf … | tee` per the channel rules — no heredoc — after `mkdir -p /etc/pihole`.

Then the password (`pihole -a -p $MASS_PASSWORD`) and a check that it resolves.

WHERE IT IS NOW — Pi-hole IS INSTALLED. Read off the machine:
  pihole-FTL is active; Core v6.4.3, Web v6.6, FTL v6.7.1; gravity loaded 74,761 domains
  `pct exec 130 -- dig +short google.com @127.0.0.1` -> 142.250.189.110  (resolving)
  /etc/pihole/pihole.toml: [dns.blocking] active = true, mode = "NULL"; interface = "eth0"; port 53; [dhcp] active = false  (DHCP correctly OFF, as this step requires)
  /etc/pihole/setupVars.conf no longer exists — v6 migrated it into pihole.toml and removed it, which is expected; do not treat its absence as a failure.

TWO THINGS REMAIN. Do not rebuild anything; finish these.

1. THE PASSWORD COMMAND FAILED ON PATH, not on Pi-hole:
     pct exec 130 -- pihole -a -p "$MASS_PASSWORD"
     lxc-attach: Failed to exec "pihole"   rc=127
   `pihole` is at /usr/local/bin/pihole and `pct exec` runs with a minimal PATH that does not include /usr/local/bin. Use the ABSOLUTE path, or a login shell (`pct exec 130 -- bash -lc '…'`). Note this is Pi-hole v6: confirm the current password subcommand rather than assuming `-a -p`, which changed in v6 — read `pihole --help` through the runner if unsure instead of guessing.

2. BLOCKING IS NOT ACTUALLY BLOCKING, even though it is enabled in config:
     pct exec 130 -- dig +short ad.doubleclick.net @127.0.0.1 -> 142.250.177.230  (a real IP)
   Gravity says 74,761 domains are loaded and [dns.blocking] active = true, so the question is WHY a query is not being filtered — not whether to re-run the installer. Diagnose it from the machine: is the domain actually in gravity (`pihole -q`), is FTL answering the query it is being asked (check its own query log), does a domain you KNOW is on StevenBlack's list get blocked. Find the cause before changing anything.

This step is done when a known-blocked domain returns the blocking reply and the admin password is set — not when the installer has run.

title: Add every public indexer Prowlarr listed, and connect it to Radarr and Sonarr
description:
ADD96's output is the authoritative list: 88 public indexer definitions this Prowlarr ships, each with its exact name, implementation and configContract. Read it from the upstream context.

WHY THE OBVIOUS APPROACH WILL NOT WORK, so do not attempt it:
  * 88 separate `curl -X POST` commands exceed the block's limit (24), so most would be silently dropped.
  * A generic shell loop over the names cannot work either: each indexer needs ITS OWN `fields` from the schema entry (baseUrl and so on), and several names contain spaces ("Bangumi Moe", "Free JAV Torrent").
  * Do not hand-write bodies from memory. The previous attempt sent `implementation: Torznab` for indexers that are actually `Cardigann`/`CardigannSettings`, and `priority: 0` which Prowlarr rejects (it must be 1-50; 25 is the default).

SO USE THE SCHEMA OBJECTS THEMSELVES. The clean way, and the one the channel can carry: write a small script to the host with `printf '%s\n' ... | tee /tmp/add_indexers.py`, then run it as a second command. Two self-contained commands, no heredoc, nothing multi-line in a single command.

The script should: fetch `GET /api/v1/indexer/schema`, keep every entry whose privacy is `public`, and for each one POST that entry back to `/api/v1/indexer` unchanged except for setting `priority` to 25 and enabling it — because the schema entry already carries the correct name, implementation, configContract and fields. Have it print one line per indexer saying added or failed with the reason, and a final count of added out of total.

The API key is `$PROWLARR_API_KEY` from the engine's store — reference it, and let the runner expand it; do not write a key into the script or ask the operator for one.

THEN connect the applications, which is small enough to do directly: add Radarr (http://192.168.1.22:7878, `$RADARR_API_KEY`) and Sonarr (http://192.168.1.23:8989, `$SONARR_API_KEY`) to `/api/v1/applications` with full sync, then trigger a sync so the indexers appear in both. Every write uses `--fail-with-body` so a rejection is not mistaken for success.

The operator asked for breadth — "public and free with largest selections", "as many as possible". Add all 88 that the list contains, not a sample, and report how many landed. Do not ask them to type an indexer name: the list is in the upstream output.

Done when Prowlarr lists the added indexers and both Radarr and Sonarr show them.

READ THE API KEYS OFF THE MACHINE, NOT FROM THE ENVIRONMENT. The operator's point, and they are right: each of these services keeps its own key in its own config file, so nothing has to be threaded into the script at all.

Measured just now:
  pct exec 102 -- ls -l /var/lib/prowlarr/config.xml  ->  513 bytes, exists
  Prowlarr runs as `/opt/Prowlarr/Prowlarr -nobrowser -data=/var/lib/prowlarr`, so its config is `/var/lib/prowlarr/config.xml` and the key is the `<ApiKey>` element in it. Radarr and Sonarr follow the same pattern in containers 103 and 104 — check their own ExecStart `-data=` path rather than assuming.

So have the script read each key itself with `pct exec <ctid> -- cat <that path>` and pull the `<ApiKey>` value out. That is better than the stored copy for three reasons worth stating: the key cannot be stale, nothing secret has to cross from the engine into the script, and the value never appears in any command, block or log.

The previous attempt failed twice on exactly this. First `python3 /tmp/add_indexers.py` with the script reading `os.environ["PROWLARR_API_KEY"]` — the runner only injects a stored value into a command that mentions it, so the variable was simply absent (`KeyError`). Then the redraft switched to `os.environ.get(...)`, which removes the error and leaves the key None, so every request would have failed 401 instead. Reading the key from the container avoids the whole question.

Do not print a key, and do not write one into a file.

THE LAST RUN GOT FURTHER THAN ANY BEFORE IT. What worked, and the two things that did not.

WORKED: the script was written, compiled and ran; `get_key(102, …)` read Prowlarr's key out of the container; the schema fetch succeeded; all 88 public definitions were attempted. Keep all of that.

FAILED 1 — EVERY POST RETURNED HTTP 400. `failed: Anidex - HTTP Error 400`, `failed: NewStudio - HTTP Error 400`, and so on for all of them. A schema entry is a TEMPLATE, not a postable body: posting `dict(entry)` back with only `priority` and `enable` set is missing what Prowlarr requires. The very first attempt at this step told us one of them —
     "propertyName": "AppProfileId", "errorMessage": "'App Profile Id' must be greater than '0'"
so the body needs a real `appProfileId`. Read the available profiles (`GET /api/v1/appprofile`) and use an actual id rather than guessing 1. Then, instead of assuming that is the only missing field, have the script PRINT the 400 response body for the first failure and stop — Prowlarr says exactly which property it rejected, and one honest error beats 88 identical ones.

FAILED 2 — a root-needing substitution inside a non-root command. Commands 3-5 were
     curl … -H "X-Api-Key: $(pct exec 102 -- cat …)"
and the inner `pct exec` ran unprivileged and was refused, even though the same `pct exec` worked fine from inside the SCRIPT. So do the application wiring in the script too: add Radarr (192.168.1.22:7878) and Sonarr (192.168.1.23:8989) and trigger the sync from Python, reading each key with the same `get_key` helper. Do not put a privileged substitution inside a `curl`.

Report the count that actually landed, and if the first POST fails, show its response body rather than looping through 88 failures.

THE BODY IS NOW CORRECT. Proof from the last run: the rejection changed from a validation complaint to
    "Unable to connect to indexer, indexer's server is unavailable. HTTP request failed: [502:BadGateway] [GET] at [https://anidex.info/...]"
Prowlarr accepted `appProfileId` and `priority` and got as far as TESTING the indexer — and anidex.info answered 502. Keep the body exactly as it is.

NOW DISTINGUISH TWO KINDS OF FAILURE. The last run stopped at the first one and so added 0 of 89 because a single dead tracker halted everything. That is wrong here:

  - A VALIDATION failure (the body is wrong -- a property named, a value out of range, a missing field) means every other add would fail the same way. STOP, print the body, fix it.
  - An AVAILABILITY failure about that ONE indexer ("unable to connect", "server is unavailable", 502, 503, timeout, DNS for that site) says nothing about the others. SKIP it, count it, and CARRY ON. Many public trackers are dead or blocked at any given moment; that is normal and is not a reason to add none.

  - "Should be unique" means the thing ALREADY EXISTS. Radarr and Sonarr are already registered as applications in Prowlarr -- that is what the last two runs were told. Treat it as already-done, not a failure, and do not fail the step over it.

Report three numbers at the end: added, already present, and unreachable -- with the names of the unreachable ones so the operator can see which sites were down rather than wondering why the count is short. The operator asked for breadth; getting most of 89 is the goal, not all-or-nothing.

title: Give the media-stack containers working DNS (point them at Pi-hole)
description:
FIVE OF SEVEN CONTAINERS HAVE NO WORKING DNS. Measured just now through the runner:

  getent hosts github.com
    host            -> 140.82.114.4   works
    101 jellyfin    -> 140.82.114.4   works
    130 pihole      -> 140.82.112.3   works  (it was given --nameserver 1.1.1.1)
    102 prowlarr    -> TIMED OUT
    103 radarr      -> TIMED OUT
    104 sonarr      -> TIMED OUT
    105 download-client -> TIMED OUT
    111 control-panel   -> TIMED OUT

  pct exec 102 -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
    # --- BEGIN PVE ---
    search tail3692cc.ts.net
    nameserver 100.100.100.100
    nameserver fd7a:115c:a1e0::53
    # --- END PVE ---

`100.100.100.100` is Tailscale's MagicDNS. Those containers inherited it from the host and it does not answer for them, so they can resolve NOTHING. This is why every one of the 88 Prowlarr indexer validations failed with "Unable to connect to indexer … Resource temporarily unavailable (anidex.info:443)" — the body was fine, the name could not be resolved. It also means Radarr, Sonarr and the download client cannot reach any tracker or metadata service, so nothing would ever download even once indexers are added.

GOAL: those five containers resolve names again, through Pi-hole at 192.168.1.30 — which is what it was set up for and needs nothing from the router.

Set the nameserver per container on the Proxmox host and confirm each one resolves afterwards. Do not change the HOST's own resolver: it works, Tailscale depends on it, and breaking it would take the engine's own channel with it.

Two things to get right:
  - Pi-hole (130) must NOT be pointed at itself in a loop; leave its own resolver alone.
  - If Pi-hole is ever down these five lose DNS, so say that plainly in the output and give them a second resolver as a fallback alongside it.

Worth telling the operator in one line: this is the part of the DNS work that IS achievable without the Spectrum app — per-container, on the host. The app only matters for devices that get their DNS from the router.

Done when all five resolve github.com, and Pi-hole's query log shows the lookups arriving.

THE EXACT FORM, because two attempts have now got it wrong. `pct set --nameserver` takes ONE argument which is a single space-separated list, QUOTED:

    pct set 102 --nameserver "192.168.1.30 1.1.1.1"

Two separate arguments gives `400 too many arguments` (attempt 1). Repeating the option -- `--nameserver 192.168.1.30 --nameserver 1.1.1.1` -- is not valid either (attempt 2). One option, one quoted value, both addresses inside the quotes. Same for all five containers.

title: Set static IP and gateway on LXC 111's net0
description: Configure container 111 (control-panel) with a static address by setting net0 to ip=192.168.1.25/24,gw=192.168.1.1 (keeping its existing bridge=vmbr0, firewall=1, and hwaddr BC:24:11:66:89:94). Done when `pct config 111` shows net0 carrying ip=192.168.1.25/24,gw=192.168.1.1 and the container can reach the gateway at 192.168.1.1.

Confirm done when PM2 reports the process online and the backend is listening on port 3001 (e.g. `pct exec 111 -- pm2 list` shows status online, and `pct exec 111 -- ss -tlnp | grep 3001` shows a LISTEN on *:3001).

title: Set static IP and gateway on LXC 111's net0
description: Configure container 111 (control-panel) with a static address by setting net0 to include ip=192.168.1.25/24 and gw=192.168.1.1 on bridge vmbr0, keeping its existing MAC BC:24:11:66:89:94 and firewall=1. Done when pct config 111 shows the net0 line carrying ip=192.168.1.25/24,gw=192.168.1.1 and the container is restarted so the new addressing takes effect.

description: Start the PM2-managed process 'control-panel-backend' (id 1) inside LXC container 111 (control-panel). Done when `pct exec 111 -- pm2 list` shows the process with status 'online' and the backend is listening on port 3001 (confirmed via `pct exec 111 -- ss -tlnp | grep :3001`).

title: Configure VM 100 for GPU passthrough and Ubuntu 22.04
description: Set VM 100's guest OS type to l26 (Linux 6.x/Ubuntu 22.04) and attach the NVIDIA GPU(s) via hostpci passthrough so the guest can use them directly. Done when `qm config 100` shows ostype: l26 and a hostpci0 line mapping the intended GPU (e.g. the Tesla P40), and the VM can be started without the host claiming the device.

title: Set nameserver 192.168.1.1 on container 101
description: Configure container 101 (jellyfin) to use 192.168.1.1 as its DNS nameserver via `pct set 101 -nameserver 192.168.1.1`. Done when `pct config 101` shows nameserver 192.168.1.1 and the container can resolve a hostname (e.g. `pct exec 101 -- getent hosts defrusciohomelab.duckdns.org` returns an address).

title: Resize VM 106's scsi0 disk to 40G
description: Grow (or recreate) VM 106 (palworld-server)'s scsi0 disk so it is 40G, matching the claimed 40G disk.
```bash
printf '\n' | timeout 8 socat -t 6 - UNIX-CONNECT:/var/run/qemu-server/106.serial0
```

title: Install Ubuntu 22.04 on VM 106 unattended (cloud image + cloud-init)
description:
VM 106 (palworld-server) has NO operating system: its only disk, local-lvm:vm-106-disk-0 (100G), has never been written (`lvs` Data% 0.00, no partition table — the engine measured this on 2026-10-02; ADD5's install was removed by ADD53's `pvesm free`). Install Ubuntu Server 22.04 on VM 106 UNATTENDED — no console interaction at any point — the Proxmox way, from the host (the runner runs here as root):

1. Download the Ubuntu 22.04 (jammy) cloud image to the host if it is not already there: `curl -fL -o /var/lib/vz/template/jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/jammy/current/jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img` (about 700 MB).
2. Stop VM 106 if it is running (`qm status 106 | grep -q running && qm stop 106`), then import the image as a new disk on local-lvm (`qm importdisk 106 /var/lib/vz/template/jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img local-lvm` — it appears as `unused0`, named vm-106-disk-1), attach it as the boot disk (`qm set 106 --scsihw virtio-scsi-pci --scsi0 local-lvm:vm-106-disk-1 --boot order=scsi0`) and grow it to 100G (`qm resize 106 scsi0 100G`; cloud-init grows the filesystem on first boot). The old empty disk vm-106-disk-0 becomes unused: detach and free it (`qm set 106 --delete unused0` after confirming which unusedN it is, then `pvesm free local-lvm:vm-106-disk-0`) — nothing is lost, it was never written.
3. Attach a cloud-init drive and seed it: `qm set 106 --ide2 local-lvm:cloudinit --ciuser aedefruscio --cipassword "$MASS_PASSWORD" --sshkeys /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub --ipconfig0 ip=dhcp --nameserver 192.168.1.1 --agent 1 --serial0 socket --vga serial0`. The password is the stored MASS_PASSWORD, referenced BY NAME exactly as written (the runner expands it; the value never appears in any block); the SSH key is this host's own public key, so the engine can log in afterwards.
4. Start VM 106 (`qm start 106`), then wait for it to come up on the network: its NIC MAC is in `qm config 106` (net0); loop up to 12 × 10 s over a sweep (`nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 >/dev/null 2>&1`) and `ip neigh show | grep -i <mac>` until an address appears, then `ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new aedefruscio@<address> 'lsb_release -ds'` until it answers (cloud-init needs a minute on first boot).

Done when that ssh prints "Ubuntu 22.04…" and `qm config 106` shows scsi0 = local-lvm:vm-106-disk-1 (100G) and ide2 = the cloud-init drive. Installing qemu-guest-agent inside the guest is ADD82's job, not this step's. The whole sequence is one bash script under ## Write these files, run as `MASS_PASSWORD="$MASS_PASSWORD" bash /tmp/<name>.sh`; every lookup a wait loop expects to be empty ends in `|| true`.

No UI yet. On container 111. Done when `pct exec 111 -- grep -n 'radarr\|sonarr' /opt/control-panel-backend/server.js` shows it.

title: Start container 120 (caddy-proxy)
description:
Container 120 (caddy-proxy) is stopped. It is the reverse proxy that serves the control panel from outside the house, which the operator has decided they want, so ADD100's build was refused until it is running.

Start it and confirm it came up. One command starts it; one read confirms it.

Done when `pct status 120` reports running.

title: Make the control-panel backend come back on its own after a reboot
description:
ADD21 tried to do this with `pct exec 111 -- pm2 start 1` and could not: read off the machine just now, `pct exec 111 -- pm2 list` prints an EMPTY table and spawning the daemon was the first thing that command did — so PM2 was not running and had no saved process list, and process id 1 never existed. `pm2 start 1` could not have worked whatever the container's state.

What IS true: the backend is serving. `pct exec 111 -- ss -tlnp` shows `node` listening on `*:3001`. It is running as a bare process, so it does NOT come back after a reboot, and that is the actual gap.

Goal: the control-panel backend starts by itself when container 111 boots, and keeps running if it crashes.

Decide the mechanism yourself and say why in one line — a systemd unit inside the container is the ordinary answer on a Debian/Ubuntu LXC and needs nothing extra installed; PM2 is fine too if it is already there for a reason. Do not ask the operator to choose between process managers; they are not expected to know the difference.

Read what is actually running before you change it — replacing a working process with a managed one must not leave the panel down. Bring the managed one up and confirm `*:3001` is still answering.

Done when the backend survives `pct reboot 111` and `*:3001` is listening again afterwards.

title: Install PalWorld server
Bring the PalWorld service (palworld.service) up on UDP 8211 inside VM 106
description: Inside VM 106 (palworld-server): the dedicated server is installed under /opt/palworld (T23, 2026-10-03, SteamCMD app 2394010, user steam) and its systemd unit is /etc/systemd/system/palworld.service (written by T23, rewritten and enabled by T24). Nothing has started it. Start it: systemctl enable --now palworld.service, then wait for the listener. Done when `systemctl is-active palworld.service` prints active and `ss -ulnp` inside the guest shows a UDP listener on port 8211.
